readingSections.title: Variables and Types: var vs let vs const, primitives, typeof and coercion
readingSections.quickSummary: var function-scoped hoisted with undefined, let block-scoped no redeclare, const block-scoped no reassign. Primitives: string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null, symbol. typeof guards type. == coerces, === strict. Falsy: false, 0, empty string, null, undefined, NaN.
content: Declare with let when the binding will change, with const when it will not be reassigned, and avoid var in new code because var is function-scoped, hoisted to undefined before its declaration line, and allows redeclaration silently. Example: for(var i=0;i<3;i++) leaks i outside the loop, while for(let i=0;i<3;i++) keeps i in the block. Temporarily dead zone means let and const cannot be read before their line — reading them early throws ReferenceError, not undefined.

Types are dynamic — one variable can hold a string and later a number. Primitives are string, number (IEEE 754 double), bigint for huge integers via trailing n, boolean, undefined (declared but not set), null (intentional empty via assignment), and symbol (unique key). Objects are the rest: Array, Object, Function, Date, RegExp, Map and Set. typeof returns a string with one classic lie: typeof null is object, which is a historic bug, not the real type.

Coercion is the exam's favourite trap. Double equals == coerces types before comparing: "5" == 5 is true, 0 == false is true, null == undefined is true, but null == 0 is false. Triple equals === is strict plus no coercion: "5" === 5 is false, null === undefined is false. Prefer strict in real code; the exam tests you know the difference by listing both results.

Falsy and truthy govern conditionals and the tiny operators. Falsy six: false, 0, negative zero, empty string, null, undefined, NaN. Everything else is truthy, including empty array and empty object and string zero. The patterns || as default (value || fallback takes fallback when value is falsy) vs && as guard (value && value.prop reads only when truthy) rely on this. The newer ?? as nullish coalescing is stricter: value ?? fallback only when value is null or undefined, not zero or empty string.

Surface quirk: NaN means not a number but its type is number: typeof NaN is number, and NaN !== NaN is true, so test via Number.isNaN. parseInt("08") and Number("  5  ") vs parseFloat differ on whitespace plus trailing junk.

subsections.title: Hoisting vs TDZ in 15 seconds
subsections.content: var declaration hoists to the top of its function as undefined. let and const hoist but sit in a dead zone until their line — access before throws. Function declarations hoist fully; function expressions and arrow assigned to let/const do not run before their line.

subsections.title: typeof lie and one-operator test
subsections.content: typeof null === "object" is the bug to remember. typeof an array is also "object" — test Array.isArray instead. For numbers prefer Number.isNaN over isNaN which coerces.

quickRevision: var function-scoped hoisted undefined and redeclare-able; let block-scoped no redeclare, const no reassign, both dead zone early.
Primitives 7 plus objects; typeof null is object bug; array test via isArray.
== coerces ("5"==5 true), === strict no coercion ("5"===5 false); null==undefined true via double but false via triple.
Falsy six: false, 0, empty string, null, undefined, NaN — everything else truthy; || default vs ?? nullish (null or undefined only).
NaN type number, NaN !== NaN true, use isNaN plus parseInt vs Number.
tricks: Any answer that says const makes an object immutable is wrong — const prevents reassignment of the binding, not mutation of object contents.
Do not swap || with ?? — || triggers on zero or empty string, ?? only on null or undefined.
0 == false is true via double, 0 === false is false via triple — exam loves this pair.
patterns: 'Hoisted var vs dead zone let/const?' -> var undefined before line, let/const throws before line.
'Falsy list?' -> false, 0, empty string, null, undefined, NaN — rest truthy.
'Coerce vs strict?' -> == coerces true for "5" vs 5, === strict false.
'Null type?' -> typeof null is object bug; array test isArray.

pyqPatterns.approach: var function undefined before, let/const dead zone throws, typeof null object lie, double coerces true, triple strict false, six falsy.

pyqPatterns.approach: || defaults on falsy six so trips on zero; ?? nullish only on null or undefined so keeps zero.

readingSections.title: Functions and Events: declarations vs expressions vs arrows, this, closures and loop capture plus event flow
readingSections.quickSummary: Function declaration hoists, expression does not, arrow has no own this and closes over call site. this at call depends on dot plus strict vs global vs arrow vs bind. Closure keeps outer after return — loop capture bug fixed by let. Events bubble up, capture down, stopPropagation stops, preventDefault cancels.
content: Functions have three faces the exam swaps. Function declaration function f(){} hoists fully so you can call above its line. Function expression const f = function(){} and arrow const f = () => {} do not hoist as callable before their assignment line — early calls fail. Arrows have no own this, no arguments object (use rest ...args), and cannot be constructors with new — parent scope this is closed over instead.

this binding has four rules the paper rotates. In sloppy mode, bare foo() gets global this (window); in strict, undefined. With a dot, obj.foo() gets obj as this. With new, new Foo() gets the new instance. With bind/call/apply, foo.bind(o) forces o. Arrow ignores all four and uses the surrounding scope this where defined — that is why arrow plus method combination is risky.

Closure means a function keeps its outer bindings after the outer has returned. Classic loop trap: for(var i=0;i<3;i++) { setTimeout(function(){console.log(i)},0) } prints 3,3,3 because var leaks and three closures share one i. Fix: for(let i=0;i<3;i++) with block-scoped i each closure gets its own, or wrap with an IIFE. Closure enables private state: function counter(){let n=0; return ()=> ++n} keeps n alive after return.

Events have capture plus target plus bubble. A click enters from the window down via capturing, fires on the target, then bubbles up through ancestors. addEventListener third arg can be true for capture or {capture:true} or {once:true} or {passive:true}. Stop flows: event.stopPropagation stops bubbling or capturing beyond; event.stopImmediatePropagation also stops other listeners on the same target; event.preventDefault cancels the default action (link navigate or form submit) without stopping flow.

Two more traps that steal marks. One, hoisting: declaration hoists, expression does not — calling an arrow above its line fails. Two, rest vs spread: ...args in a parameter is rest that gathers many into an array, ...arr in a call is spread that explodes an array into many arguments — same dots, opposite direction.

subsections.title: this decision order that survives pressure
subsections.content: Is it an arrow? Arrow uses surrounding this, not call site. New? new instance. Bound via bind/call/apply? bound object. Dotted call obj.foo()? obj. Bare strict? undefined; bare sloppy? global. That order answers every this MCQ.

subsections.title: Closure plus async loop in one sight
subsections.content: Loop plus async inside plus var is the signature of the triple-3 bug. One let per iteration fixes it because each turn gets its own i. IIFE that captures the current var also fixes in legacy code, but AXIS rewards let.

quickRevision: Declaration hoists callable, expression and arrow not before line. Arrow no own this plus no arguments plus not a constructor.
this via new > bind/call/apply > dot obj > bare global/undefined; arrow overrides and closes over surrounding.
Closure keeps outer after outer returns; var loop shares one i (3,3,3), let gives per-iteration copy fixes.
Capture down then target then bubble up; stopPropagation stops flow, preventDefault cancels default, immediate also kills other listeners on target.
Rest gathers in definition (...args array), spread explodes in call (...arr many). Hoisting declaration yes, expression/arrow no.
tricks: Any answer that says an arrow has its own this via call site is wrong — arrow closes over surrounding scope.
Do not confuse stopPropagation with preventDefault — first stops travel, second cancels the default action but not travel.
Barest this confusion: sloppy vs strict differs only for bare calls — dotted calls dominate both.
patterns: 'Declaration hoists callable?' -> Yes. 'Expression/arrow before line?' -> No.
'Arrow own this?' -> No own; uses surrounding.
'Loop var plus async prints 3,3,3 vs let fixes?' -> Var shares, let per turn. 'Closure private counter?' -> Function returning function keeps var alive.
'Capture vs bubble?' -> Capture down, bubble up. 'Stop travel vs cancel click?' -> stopPropagation vs preventDefault.

pyqPatterns.question: Hoisting vs arrow this vs closure loop capture plus events bubble vs capture vs stop?
pyqPatterns.approach: Declaration hoists arrow not, arrow no own this, var loop 3,3,3 vs let per turn, capture down bubble up stop vs prevent.

pyqPatterns.question: Gather many into an array vs explode an array into many — dots in definition vs call?
pyqPatterns.approach: Rest gathers in definition (...args array), spread explodes in call (...arr many).

readingSections.title: DOM Basics: tree, selection, nodes vs elements, create and mutation vs XSS
readingSections.quickSummary: DOM is the live tree of the page: Document at root, Elements as tags plus Nodes vs Elements distinction, HTMLCollection live vs NodeList. Select via getElementById/ByClass vs querySelectorAll. Create via createElement plus append. textContent safe vs innerHTML risky (XSS). Events bubble through it; styles via classList and style.
content: The DOM (Document Object Model) is the browser's live tree view of the page. Root is Document, children are Elements (tags), which own Attributes, have Text Nodes, and are shaped by CSSOM and layout. The DOM is live — changes via scripts repaint immediately. The exam word live is not filler — live collections update as the document changes.

Selecting elements has two families. Classic: getElementById returns one, getElementsByClassName and getElementsByTagName return a live HTMLCollection that auto-updates on DOM mutation, and getElementsByName returns by name attribute. Modern: querySelector returns the first matching CSS selector, querySelectorAll returns a static NodeList snapshot that does not track DOM changes. The exam swaps live vs static — that is the free mark many pilots miss.

Nodes vs Elements is the other discriminant. Node includes everything: Element nodes, Text nodes (whitespace counts), Comment nodes. Element is the subset that are tags. NodeList can hold both kinds; HTMLCollection holds Elements only. childNodes includes all nodes including text whitespace; children includes only Element children — that one-versus text trick reappears under box model too.

Creating and mutating: document.createElement("div") builds an element, document.createTextNode builds a text node, parent.appendChild(child) and parent.append(element, text) attach, parent.insertBefore(new, existing), parent.replaceChild(new, old), oldClone = node.cloneNode(deep) deep vs shallow, and remove via node.remove() or parent.removeChild(child). Attribute via setAttribute plus getAttribute plus removeAttribute; CSS class manipulation via classList.add/remove/toggle and style via element.style (inline) or getComputedStyle for the real rendered value.

Safety: textContent sets plain text safely — no HTML is parsed. innerHTML parses as HTML and can lead to XSS (cross-site scripting) if user input is inserted via innerHTML without sanitization. The exam writes innerHTML equals userInput and asks which is unsafe — answer innerHTML without escaping. Events emitted by the DOM bubble or capture through the tree exactly as the functions section described.

subsections.title: Live vs static in one glance
subsections.content: Live HTMLCollection via getElementsByClassName auto-updates when you add or remove elements of that class. Static NodeList via querySelectorAll is a snapshot — adding after does not appear until you query again. That is why a loop over a live collection that mutates the collection can behave unexpectedly while a static snapshot does not.

subsections.title: textContent vs innerHTML safety rule
subsections.content: Use textContent for user-supplied text. Use innerHTML only for trusted markup or sanitized strings. Anytime the paper writes userInput into innerHTML as template it is an XSS bait — flag it.

quickRevision: DOM live tree: Document root plus Elements plus Attributes plus Text plus Comment nodes; live updates as scripts mutate.
Selectors: Classic live HTMLCollection (getElementsBy*) vs Modern static NodeList (querySelectorAll). getElementById one, querySelector first, querySelectorAll many.
Nodes vs Elements: Node includes Elements plus Text plus Comments; Element subset that are tags; childNodes all vs children only elements.
Mutation via createElement plus append plus insertBefore plus replaceChild plus cloneNode plus remove plus setAttribute plus classList plus style. Live collections react.
textContent safe plain, innerHTML parses HTML risky XSS if userInput via innerHTML; events bubble through.
tricks: Any answer that says querySelectorAll returns a live collection is wrong — it is static NodeList vs live HTMLCollection for getElementsBy*.
Do not swap childNodes with children — childNodes includes Text whitespace, children Elements only.
innerHTML plus user input without escaping is the XSS flag — always choose textContent for untrusted data.
patterns: 'One element vs first vs many?' -> getElementById one, querySelector first, querySelectorAll many (static). 'Live updating collection?' -> getElementsByClassName HTMLCollection.
'Tag vs everything?' -> Element vs Node (Node includes Text and Comments). 'Live vs static after DOM change?' -> Live vs NodeList.
'Build and attach?' -> createElement plus append, insertBefore, replaceChild, cloneNode, remove, classList add or remove.
'User text safe vs HTML parse risky?' -> textContent safe plain vs innerHTML parses risky XSS.

pyqPatterns.approach: Classic getElementsBy* live HTMLCollection vs querySelectorAll static NodeList, Nde plus Text vs Element, childNodes vs children.

readingSections.title: ES6 Highlights: arrow, let/const, template literals, destructuring, spread/rest, default, modules, promises and async or await plus classes
readingSections.quickSummary: ES6 modern syntax: let/const, arrow, template `${}` literals, destructuring of objects and arrays, spread vs rest `...`, default params, modules import/export, Promise plus chaining then vs catch, async/await syntax sugar. Transpile via Babel when old browsers must run new syntax; bundle via bundlers.
content: let and const were covered but the ES6 context adds why: block scope plus const binding were added to fix var leaking and to enable tooling to reason about immutability at the binding level — not object immutability. Use const by default and fall back to let only when reassignment is needed. The exam writes var vs let vs const with reassignment plus block plus loop capture and expects the trade-off wording.

Arrow plus template: arrow () => {} omits its own this plus arguments; template literals via backticks allow `${expr}` interpolation plus multiline strings. Destructuring extracts: const {name, age} = person and const [a,b] = arr plus nested plus defaults. Default parameters function f(name = "Asha") give fallback even when undefined is passed; combine with destructuring for options bags: function f({x=0, y=0}={}).

Spread vs rest unify with `...`. Spread explodes an array or object in a call or literal: fn(...arr) and [...arr, 4] and {...a, ...b} spread merges objects. Rest gathers many into an array in a definition: function f(...args) and const [first, ...rest] = arr. Same dots, opposite directions — spread call-side explosion, rest definition-side gathering.

Modules remove globals. Scripts without modules pollute window. Modules via import/export are static plus tree-shakeable: import {foo} from "./foo.js" statically declares dependencies so bundlers can drop unused exports. Type script adds types on top but for AXIS JS the paper only tests import/export existence plus transpilation via Babel plus bundling via Webpack or Vite or Rollup.

Promises model future values. A Promise has three states: pending, fulfilled with a value, rejected with a reason. Attach via then for success and catch for failure; finally always. Promise.all waits for all promises and fails on the first reject; allSettled waits for all and returns each outcome; any returns the first fulfilled; race returns first settled whether fulfill or reject. Async and await are syntax sugar on promises — await pauses the async function until the promise settles without blocking the thread, but it can only be used inside an async function (or at top-level in modules). Error handling is try plus await plus catch or await plus .catch plus finally.

subsections.title: Spread vs rest direction test
subsections.content: Dots in a function parameter plus destructuring left side is rest gathering. Dots in a function call plus array or object literal is spread explosion. The exam prints ...x in both spots and swaps labels — read where the dots sit, call vs definition.

subsections.title: Modules vs scripts in one line each
subsections.content: Script runs globally and hoists into window — bad for big apps. Module imports only what it needs via import, exports via export, scopes per file, static so tooling can tree-shake. Babel transpiles new syntax to old for old browsers; bundlers chop many files into few for delivery.

quickRevision: let/const block plus const binding-not-object; arrow no own this; template via backticks plus ${} plus multiline.
Destructuring extracts plus defaults; spread explodes in calls ({...a,...b} for objects), rest gathers in definitions (...args array).
Modules import vs export static per file vs scripts global — tree-shakeable; transpile via Babel; bundle via Webpack or Vite.
Promise pending to fulfilled/rejected via then plus catch plus finally; all vs allSettled vs any vs race; async/await sugar pauses inside async only.
Default params function f(name="Asha") plus options-bag {x=0,y=0} with destructuring.
tricks: Any answer that says const makes objects immutable is backwards — only the binding reassignment is blocked.
Do not confuse spread vs rest — call explosion vs definition gathering have opposite labels despite same dots.
all vs allSettled vs any vs race is a four-way: all waits all and fails first reject, allSettled waits all and always returns per-outcome, any first fulfilled, race first settled of any kind.
patterns: 'No own this vs own this?' -> Arrow no own closes over vs declaration own via call rules.
'Gather many into one array?' -> Rest ...args in definition 'Explode one array into many?' -> Spread ...arr in call.
'Pending to fulfilled vs rejected plus chain?' -> Promise then/catch/finally; all vs allSettled vs any vs race.
'Static per file plus tree shaking vs global polluting?' -> Modules vs scripts.

pyqPatterns.approach: Rest gathers in definition, spread explodes in call, arrow no own this, all failures differ for all vs any vs race, modules static vs scripts global.

pyqPatterns.approach: function f({x=0,y=0}={}) — fallback to default object and per-field defaults via destructuring.

readingSections.title: Exam JavaScript Synthesis (how AXIS mixes all four families)
readingSections.quickSummary: Vars vs scope vs hoist vs coercion vs falsy first. Functions plus this plus closures plus loop capture plus capture vs bubble vs stop vs prevent second. DOM selection plus live vs static plus nodes vs elements vs textContent vs innerHTML XSS third. ES6 arrow plus spread vs rest plus template plus modules plus promise combinators plus async or await fourth. One pass per verb kills most tables.
content: Vars row: var function undefined before vs let/const dead zone throws plus const binding not object plus typeof null is object bug vs isArray plus double coerces vs triple strict plus OR default vs nullish coalesce only null or undefined plus falsy six plus NaN !== NaN.

Functions plus events row: declaration hoists callable vs expression/arrow not before vs arrow no own this vs bound/call/apply vs dot vs bare strict plus closure keeps outer after return plus var loop 3,3,3 vs let per turn plus rest gather in definition vs spread explode in call plus capture down vs bubble up vs stopPropagation vs preventDefault.

DOM row: classic live HTMLCollection vs modern static NodeList vs getElementById one vs querySelector first vs querySelectorAll many static vs nodes with Text/Comment vs elements tag vs childNodes all vs children elements plus create via createElement plus append plus insertBefore vs clone vs remove plus classList plus safety textContent safe vs innerHTML XSS via user input.

ES6 row: let/const plus arrow plus template with backticks plus destructuring with defaults plus spread vs rest via dots direction plus modules static import/export plus transpilation vs bundling plus Promise pending-fulfilled-rejected via then/catch/finally plus combinators all vs allSettled vs any vs race plus async/await sugar inside async with try/catch plus classes as syntactic sugar over prototypes.

Speed rule for the exam hall: any mixed JavaScript table with five stems is solved by one pass — read var scope vs type vs coercion vs function hoist vs arrow this vs DOM live vs spread direction vs promise fail policy. Circle the discriminant word in each stem and the distractors neutralize.

subsections.title: One-pass elimination for hard mixed items
subsections.content: Item offers both var vs let vs const with "reassign the object" bait — eliminate reassignable via const if the check is mutation vs binding. Item offers || vs ?? bait — eliminate || if the check is zero must stay. Item offers arrow vs declaration for an early call — pick declaration.

subsections.title: When both DOM and events appear together
subsections.content: Selector family decides live vs static; bubble vs capture decides direction; stop vs prevent decides travel vs default. Keep rows separate — DOM models the tree, events travel it.

quickRevision: Vars falsy vs scope vs hoist vs coercion vs typeof vs ??? are the six micro-tests for the vars row.
Declaration hoists callable vs expression/arrow not; arrow no own this, closure loop var 3,3,3 vs let per. use rest gather def vs spread call, capture down bubble up stop vs prevent.
HTMLCollection live vs NodeList static; nodes-plus-text vs elements tags; childNodes all vs children elements; textContent safe vs innerHTML XSS via userInput.
Spread explode vs rest gather; Promise all vs allSettled vs any vs race; modules static vs scripts global.
One pass per discriminant word solves most mixed tables.
tricks: Any answer that says const freezes an object is wrong — reassignment is blocked, mutation is allowed.
Do not swap querySelectorAll live vs static — it is static NodeList that later inserts do not affect until re-queried.
All vs any vs race is not three synonyms — all waits all and fails first reject, any first fulfill, race first settled of any kind, allSettled always per-outcome.
patterns: 'Binding reuse vs object mutation?' -> const binding not object.
'Early call before line?' -> Declaration hoists, expression/arrow does not.
'Live updating collection after add?' -> Live HTMLCollection yes vs static NodeList no.
'Any fail rejects first vs waits always?' -> all vs allSettled.
'Prevent link navigate vs stop bubble?' -> preventDefault vs stopPropagation.

Triple equals no coercion: "5" === 5 false, null === undefined false. Prefer strict in real code.
